w: Dr. Geurs taught this in class, the week after Dr. Litz's lecture on bone-reshaping surgery. (He'd rather have gone first: when you see a defect, "your first thought should be regeneration.") He had two goals for you: spot the bone defects that can be regrown, and know what treatment can do for them. You won't learn to do this surgery in dental school (it takes a specialist's training, such as a perio residency); your job is to recognize these defects, know they can save the tooth, and refer. These notes follow the class, with his slides and the class review guide. What regeneration means Periodontal regeneration means growing back all three parts of the tooth's attachment: new bone, new cementum (the thin layer on the root) and new periodontal ligament (the fibers that hold the tooth in the bone), on a root that gum disease had stripped bare. In his words, they are "three different tissues that have to all regenerate in harmony with each other. It can't just be bone alone." If only bone came back, something else would sit between the bone and the root. The opposite is repair: healing that closes the wound but doesn't rebuild the original structure. After a flap or a deep cleaning, the root usually just repairs: a long strip of gum lining, a long junctional epithelium, sticks to the root, and a gap lined with gum lining is a pocket again. First, a clean root His first case was a molar with a deep vertical (infrabony) defect: bone lost down along the side of the root, with a deep pocket beside it. The first problem in that hole is bacteria. The root had tartar (calculus) on it, and wherever there's tartar there are bacteria. Tartar is rough and hard to clean, and the worst gum-disease bacteria can live right on it, against the root, without the "early" bacteria that normally have to stick first. So the root has to be cleaned, and the way to do that is scaling and root planing, the deep cleaning. ("If you want to answer a question right in perio, the answer is scaling and root planing.") It's usually done first without surgery; then, during the regeneration surgery, the flap lets you see the root and finish the job. "The most important thing to understand is that it has to be clean." How do you know the cleaning is done? You watch how the gum responds. That's different from a filling, which you can check the moment you finish. Gum treatment changes the bacteria, and the patient's own healing does the rest: once there's nothing left to fight, the inflammation goes away. The soft tissue sitting in the hole isn't ligament (that's gone) and isn't bone. It's granulomatous tissue, the diseased tissue (not the same as granulation tissue, which is healing tissue). It has to be scraped out: left there, it won't turn into bone and it blocks new bone from growing in. Cleaning it out uncovers the hole's bone walls, and those walls help the new tissue fill in. The race for the space If you just lift the gum, clean the hole and stitch the gum back, whichever tissue grows in fastest "will win the race to the space." That's the gum's lining, the epithelium: it slides straight down the root faster than anything else. Bone heals slowly but very reliably, as long as it's kept still: a broken leg in a cast takes about six weeks, a cut on your hand about a week, and an implant held still by its threads heals into the bone. If the gum lining gets to the bottom of the hole first, you have a pocket again, where bacteria grow out of reach. So regeneration is about keeping the gum lining out and helping the slow tissues win. There are many ways to steer that healing: keep the gum lining out, use drugs, even switch on genes that help bone heal, though the drug and gene ideas haven't worked well for gums yet. Put simply, it takes four things: cells, a scaffold for the cells to crawl over (cells may not cross an empty gap; a bone graft is one scaffold), growth factors, and a blood supply. A growth factor is a signal that tells cells to heal: platelets burst open in a wound and release one called PDGF, which helps cells live longer, work harder and move faster. Placed in a hole, it boosts the bone, but also the gum tissue around it. Bone also holds growth signals of its own, and cleaning it releases some, though not enough to reach all the way across the hole; a graft can help. The slides' map splits the approaches in two: tissue engineering brings in cells (grown in a lab, or seeded onto a scaffold, which can even be 3D printed), and endogenous regeneration adds no cells and calls the patient's own cells to the spot. Grafts, membranes and biologic gels work with the patient's own cells; a graft of the patient's own bone may bring a few along. Which holes regrow: walls, angle and depth Bone holes beside the root (intrabony defects) are sorted by how many bone walls are left around them, how wide they are and how deep they are. A part surrounded by three walls is a 3-wall defect, and almost every hole mixes types. His first case, once cleaned out, had about 3 mm of 3-wall hole at the bottom, then 4 to 6 mm of 2-wall hole with no wall on the cheek side, and a 1-wall part near the top. More walls means the hole is more contained: whatever you put in stays put, and there's more bone surface to help it heal. "Potentially the most amenable to regeneration are the three wall defects, the most contained ones." The angle of the walls matters too: a steep, narrow hole fills in better, but it's harder to get instruments into, so there's a sweet spot. And depth matters: a shallow hole might regrow, but other treatments usually work more reliably for it. His summary: "more walls, better. An angle that is more steep is better. And the depth of the defect is also important." Bone that has worn down flat (horizontal bone loss) can't be regrown: "There's just no defect to fill." The slide behind that summary gives the numbers: holes deeper than 3 mm, with walls at an angle of 25 degrees or less on the X-ray, do best. A hole with mostly one wall is called non-supportive and is a big risk for failure, and a 1-wall hole plus thin, scalloped gums predicted more gum recession on the front of the tooth after surgery. The list of studies on that slide is just his evidence; he said it's "not there for you to read all these studies." A 2021 review on the next slide agrees: deeper, narrower holes with more walls gain more attachment and bone. Furcations, the bone between a molar's roots, are harder. Only the bottom of a furcation is bone; the rest is root. A clean root lets new tissue grow across it, but a root never supplies cells. He called it "a dead surface in healing," and that's why furcations are harder to treat. Finding the hole before surgery You don't open the gum to decide whether a hole can be regrown: you decide from your probing measurements and X-rays. The chart shows where the deep pockets are. X-rays are trickier than you'd think. For bone loss to be easy to see on an X-ray, more than half of the bone's mineral must already be gone, and for most gum defects that means the cheek-side or tongue-side wall is gone: "by the time we see it on the radiograph, it likely is not a three-wall defect." The best holes for regrowing are the ones that probe deep (say 8 mm) while the X-ray shows only a faint shadow. An X-ray is a flat picture of a 3-D hole; the slides' X-rays of 3-, 2- and 1-wall holes on the same skull molar look surprisingly alike. So you only really count the walls during surgery, once the gum is lifted and the hole is cleaned out. The risk checklist and the decision tree A 2023 risk checklist rates each case low, medium or high risk in four areas. The patient: healthy healing or not; smoking (none is low, 10 a day or fewer is medium, more than 10 is high); plaque left on the teeth (15% or less is low, 16 to 24% medium, 25% or more high); showing up for maintenance; and realistic hopes. The tooth: its overall gum risk; whether bite trauma and looseness can be controlled; the nerve (a healthy nerve with the hole not reaching the root tip, or a good root canal, is low; an existing root canal needs a careful look; a hole reaching the root tip, a poor root canal or a dead nerve is high); the root surface (flat is low, dented medium, two fused roots high); healthy gum or not; and gum thickness (thick is low, thin with at least 2 mm of firm gum medium, thin with little or none high). The defect: 3-wall, narrow and deep is low, 2-wall medium, 1-wall, wide and shallow high; no furcation is low, Class I or II medium, Class III high; it must be reachable to clean during surgery (front teeth easiest); and a contained hole, touching 1 or 2 sides of the root, is low, while one touching 3 or more sides is high. The surgeon: experience, stress, and whether they use a checklist. The decision tree from the AAP Regeneration Workshop is in the handout, and he said to study it. Its message: understand your defect (how deep the pocket is, what the bone looks like, how many walls), then pick the treatment. First, fix the patient: uncontrolled medical problems, smoking and other habits, and poor cleaning at home. Then, after the first round of treatment, check the pockets, bleeding, looseness, the bone and any other dental work. A bone hole under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case: pockets of 5 mm or less without bleeding get non-surgical care; deeper pockets get bone-reshaping surgery. For a hole 3 mm or deeper, the best odds go 3-wall, then circumferential or 2-wall, then 1-wall, and narrow beats wide. If the tooth's outlook is poor, it comes out and gets replaced. Otherwise the hole decides the treatment: a narrow 3-wall or circumferential hole (under 2 mm wide) gets a bone graft, a membrane or a biologic; a wide one (3 mm or more) or a 2-wall hole gets a reinforced membrane, a graft plus a membrane, or a graft plus a biologic; a 1-wall hole gets combination therapy or a bone graft that contains living cells. Looks matter too: if the patient shows a lot of gum when smiling, has thin gums or has lost the gum between the teeth, go ahead only if they accept the risk to looks, skip the membrane, and think about a gum graft. The toolbox, and what it has to beat The options are bone grafts, guided tissue regeneration (GTR), combination therapy, biologics such as enamel matrix proteins or PDGF, and the surgery itself, including MIST, a minimally invasive surgery done through a small flap that keeps the gum between the teeth. Regeneration rebuilds lost support; the resective surgery from Session 5 works with what's left and reshapes the bone to get rid of the pocket. To him, how the surgery is done matters most. Most of the research is paid for by companies and is about their products (grafts, membranes), so there's little on surgical technique: getting the gum out of the way, getting in to clean the hole and see it, filling it, and closing without cutting off the blood supply. "Open the door, put stuff in, close the door." The less you open, the more blood supply you keep. The starting point to beat is open flap debridement: lift the gum, clean the hole, close it, with no graft. That alone gives a little bone at the bottom of the hole and a little attachment, "almost guaranteed... a millimeter." In the studies on the slide, pockets of about 7 mm came down to about 4 mm, with about 1.5 mm of attachment gained and about 1 mm of bone. The pocket shrank by 3 mm but the attachment improved by only 1.5 mm, because the rest is the gum shrinking down the root (recession). Any regeneration treatment has to do better than this, and today's do. A bone graft: the canine case A lower canine had a vertical defect. It had a root canal with two canals, which is unusual for a lower canine; two canals mean two roots that grew together, usually into an H-shaped root with a groove (concavity) in it. At surgery, through a small flap, he found a 3-wall part and a 2-wall part, and a streak of tartar in the groove: a hard spot for the patient to clean, and the reason the hole was there. The root canal wasn't what made the tooth fixable. You don't need a root canal to regrow bone: "generally for a tooth to do regeneration, all you need is clean roots." A root canal is only needed if the nerve is in trouble, as it can be when the hole reaches toward the root tip. He filled the hole with DFDBA (demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft): donor bone, ground into particles, with its minerals removed to uncover the bone-growth protein (bone morphogenetic protein) inside it. So it's a scaffold for bone to grow over and also a growth signal that calls bone in, and the body treats it like bone. He stitched the gum back over it to protect the graft and the blood clot from bacteria, and the tooth wasn't moving: like a broken bone, a hole heals when it's kept still. Sometimes he does a case like this without the deep cleaning first, because the cleaning shrinks the gum and leaves less of it to cover the graft. The result (in 1993) was a shallow pocket that's easy to keep clean, and the hole filled in on the X-ray: a vertical defect turned into a flat (horizontal) one. That's the goal, to fill the hole, not to grow bone all the way back to where it started. It changed the tooth's outlook, and a canine is worth saving: it's "the cornerstone of the dentition," guiding the bite so the other teeth aren't overloaded ("canines are gold"). Because of the groove, this patient should use a small interdental brush, which spreads into it, not floss, which stretches across the groove and misses it. Membranes (GTR) and combination therapy GTR rigs the race for the space. The healing power is in the hole (bone, and a little ligament at the bottom), but those are the slow tissues; the fast ones are in the gum. So a barrier membrane goes between the hole and the gum, keeping out the gum's lining and connective tissue, so the tissues we want fill the hole. The first studies, in the early 1980s, wrapped lab filters around teeth and showed bone could grow back; when he was in dental school, he was taught it couldn't. Early membranes had to be removed later; today's collagen membranes dissolve on their own. His patient Jeffrey had a deep hole (a 10 mm pocket) and a bony bump (exostosis) on the cheek side of the same area. Dr. Geurs shaved off the bump, packed that bone into the hole and covered it with a membrane: combination therapy, a scaffold (and maybe some living cells) under a membrane. A graft under a membrane also holds the space open so the membrane can't sag into the hole. The gum between the teeth didn't fully come back: lifting gum off a tooth and putting it back leaves a little recession, especially between teeth. The hole filled in, and it was still filled on X-rays at 1, 20 and 25 years. On the later X-rays the top of the bone looks crisp and dense (a crestal lamina dura), a sign of calm, stable bone; a fuzzy top means the bone is active and wearing away. (Seeing Jeffrey every three months for years, his dental team was the first to notice his memory slipping: dentists see patients more often than doctors do.) The patient's own bone is used in small bits, scraped off as bone dust or ground in a bone mill, and not processed, since it's the patient's own. Fresh bone from another person, used in the 1970s, passed on disease; with today's processed donor grafts, that isn't documented. Some people add antibiotics to the harvested bone, but a good blood clot does that job. Is your own bone better? "My conventional thinking was always yes, but the evidence doesn't really support that": processed donor bone uncovers its growth protein better and goes in clean, while bone scraped in the mouth may be contaminated. It's a toss-up. He likes using the patient's own bone because it's already there, and nobody pays for a bottle. Biologic gels Enamel matrix derivative (EMD) copies how a tooth's root forms in the embryo (Hertwig's root sheath). Its proteins, mostly amelogenins, the proteins that build enamel and the tooth's attachment while the tooth develops, are taken from the developing teeth of miniature pigs, which are genetically close to us, then processed. Put in a hole, they start a healing chain like the one in development, and he has seen "amazing healing" from EMD alone, with no bone graft. Alone or with a graft, it works about as well as GTR. Because it comes from pigs, you must tell the patient and get their consent (some religions avoid pork; religious leaders have weighed in, but it's each patient's choice). The same goes for anything from a donor: say what it is and why, call it a "processed donor product," and let the patient decide. A colleague who used donor skin in a priest without telling him had to take it back out. One EMD patient, in 2022, had almost no bone left around a very loose tooth. "Mobility is not a good thing during healing": a tooth that moves won't heal, like a broken leg without its cast. So he splinted the tooth to its neighbors with tooth-colored filling material on the tongue side, then put EMD in the hole. She didn't come back until a wisdom tooth abscess years later, and the bone was still there. Dr. Litz, back when he was a resident, treated the first case with Dr. Geurs: EMD on the root and mixed into DFDBA that filled the hole, with the gum closed over it. At two and a half months the X-ray showed little, because demineralized bone has no calcium and doesn't show until the body heals around it; later X-rays showed the fill. The gum shrank a little, mostly over the 1-wall parts. The result was a shallow pocket, a tooth that can be kept, though a spot where food gets stuck. From the class review guide: rhPDGF-BB is a lab-made growth factor that calls in bone and ligament cells, makes them multiply and helps new blood vessels grow, and it comes with a beta-TCP scaffold, a bone-friendly framework that keeps the gum from collapsing into the hole and holds the clot steady. Grafts are named by where they come from: autograft, from the patient; allograft, from another person (DFDBA); xenograft, from an animal, such as cow bone; and alloplast, a man-made material such as beta-tricalcium phosphate. Holes without walls. When a defect has no walls to contain it, nothing holds up the gum or the clot, so a biologic gel alone has little room to work. These defects usually get a graft too, to support the gum, which is why the decision tree sends a 1-wall hole to combination therapy. Keep the tooth or place an implant? Implants work well, but "a natural tooth is almost always better than an implant, unless you can't keep the tooth." A tooth saved by regeneration may last another 20 or 30 years, putting off an implant until treatment may be even better, and it keeps later options open. When an implant fails, the patient says "your implant isn't working," and fixing one failure can eat up what the next seven implant cases earned. Patients want their teeth, not implants. A gum specialist only gets to treat these holes when a general dentist spots them and refers the patient. What you can achieve, and how you know The slides show four mixes healing on X-rays over 3 to 16 months: Emdogain with donor bone, a membrane with the patient's own bone, rhPDGF with donor bone, and donor bone alone. All started as vertical defects, and donor bone, the patient's own bone or both can all regrow the attachment, if the surgery is done well. There are three ways to check: histology (looking at the tissue under a microscope), clinical measurements (probing) and X-rays. "The real evaluation of regeneration should be histological," but very few patients agree to it, so probing and X-rays stand in. Only histology can show new cementum, new ligament fibers and new bone, so only histology proves real regeneration. A probe can't tell new attachment from a strip of gum lining stuck to the root, and an X-ray shows bone, not attachment. Subtraction radiography takes two matching X-rays from different times, flips one and lays it over the other, so whatever stayed the same cancels out and only the change shows; it's the research that brought Dr. Geurs to Birmingham. In one of his studies, a patient with a tooth that couldn't be saved let them regrow its bone first, then remove the tooth for an implant. A small notch cut in the root at the tartar line, where there had been no bone, now had new ligament, new bone and a little new cementum: proof, under the microscope, that regeneration works in people. The new ligament isn't quite like the original, but it works and holds up over time. So, his two goals. When can you regrow bone? In vertical defects: deep, contained holes with walls. What can you expect? The hole fills in and the pocket gets shallow and easy to keep clean, which changes the tooth's future. Look for these in your practice, and keep teeth as long as you can.
